As of 158 PM EST Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A cold front will continue crossing the region 
this afternoon, with increasing winds and partly cloudy skies 
following in its wake. A trailing secondary front will follow 
along later this evening, ushering in a much colder airmass for 
Tuesday. A few showers will be possible as these fronts move 
through, but any precipitation will be light in nature. Winds 
will remain breezy overnight, limiting radiational cooling, but 
still expect lows to be in the 20s in most spots tonight. 

Winds gradually abate on Tuesday as high pressure builds over 
the region. We should see clearing skies as well. Highs will 
range from the low 30s to around 40F, which will definitely be a
bit of a shock after our recent warm weather. Clear skies and 
light winds will be optimal for radiational cooling Tuesday 
night, so expect temperatures to dip into the teens and low 20s 
areawide, with a few of the cold spots perhaps seeing single 
digits. Wednesday will be a beautiful late November day with 
ample sunshine, light winds, and highs in the mid 30s to mid 
40s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A low pressure system will develop near Florida 
Wednesday, tracking up the Eastern Seaboard and into our region 
the night of Thanksgiving through Friday. Even though plenty of 
uncertainty remains, a few things have become clear by this 
point. The preceding airmass has continued to trend warmer, 
especially in the 900-600 mb range, with temperatures there now 
expected to stay above freezing. Therefore, any snow from the 
main event is very unlikely. It also looks like the full warm 
sector will not reach the region, so the precipitation will 
mostly fall as a relatively cold rain, with temperatures in the 
30s and 40s. At the onset, there will be a very dry airmass, so 
there will be significant wet-bulb cooling. The coldest air 
looks to be in the 1,000-3,000 ft range and soundings show that 
this layer should fall below freezing in places at the onset of 
the precipitation. Therefore, a period of sleet and freezing 
rain is possible at this elevation for the first couple hours, 
even if temperatures before the precip are well above freezing. 
It should be helped by strong dynamical cooling as well. Because
the surface low will be to the south, northerly winds look to 
persist at the surface well into the storm for many areas and 
prevent efficient surface warm-air advection despite strong 
southeasterly winds aloft. There is also a threat for strong 
winds. A strong southeasterly/easterly low-level jet will move 
overhead, with 60-70 KT likely at around the summit level. 

By this point, models have mostly converged on the idea of the 
storm track. The low looks to get pulled north or slightly 
northwest and angle into the Appalachian Mountains and eastern 
Great Lakes. A secondary low should eventually form to the east 
near the Gulf of Maine and head out into the Canadian Maritimes.
The warm air- advection should change over any front end 
freezing rain or sleet to plain rain within a few hours and no 
significant travel impacts are expected due to wintry 
precipitation. The low level jet enters the region Thursday 
night and looks to drop down to around 5,000 ft in the in the 
northern Greens but down to around 3,000-4000 ft in the southern
Greens. Summit winds will be very strong, and gusty downslope 
winds will be possible along the western slopes of the southern 
Greens. 

The center of this low and the upper level low to the west will
move overhead going into Friday and the weekend, bringing 
scattered to numerous showers. The air aloft will notably cool, 
and this means temperatures in the mountains should eventually 
fall below freezing. Therefore, it should end as mountain snow 
showers but by that point, most of the moisture and 
precipitation will likely have exited to the east so any 
accumulations should be minimal. Also, without antecedent 
snowpack and relatively dry antecedent conditions, there is no 
significant hydro threat during the system.
